facts.statehood_note: Made from the Southwest Territory (the "Territory of the United States South of the River Ohio"), land North Carolina gave to the federal government in 1790.

symbols.name: Passion flower (maypop), first chosen by schoolchildren in 1919

facts.name_origin: From Tanasi, a Cherokee town on the Little Tennessee River in present-day Monroe County. In 1567 the Spanish explorer Juan Pardo wrote down a village called "Tanasqui." The meaning of the word is uncertain.

government.chambers: Tennessee Senate (33 members, 4-year terms) and Tennessee House of Representatives (99 members, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; no more than two terms in a row). The lieutenant governor presides over the Senate. The General Assembly itself elects the Secretary of State, State Treasurer, and Comptroller of the Treasury.
government.courts: Tennessee Supreme Court (5 justices), with two intermediate appeals courts below it: the Court of Appeals (civil cases) and the Court of Criminal Appeals, 12 judges each
government.local: 95 counties, each with a county seat; the state is also divided into three Grand Divisions (East, Middle, and West Tennessee)
government.constitution: Current constitution adopted in 1870 (earlier ones in 1796 and 1834). The 1870 constitution was written to undo Reconstruction policies, including by limiting Black citizens' voting rights; it has been amended since.
government.kid_line: "The Governor shall be elected to hold office for four years and until a successor is elected and qualified." (Article III, Section 4)

long_ago.about: People reached Tennessee by about 13,000 years ago. They lived in small family groups of 25 to 50 people and hunted mammoth, mastodon, and giant bison; a Middle Tennessee site has mastodon bones cut with stone tools.
From about 1000 to 1600, Mississippian chiefdoms built many ceremonial structures across Tennessee. They were ancestors of the Muscogee (Creek).
When Hernando de Soto's Spanish expedition came through (1539-1543), Muscogee and Yuchi people lived in the Tennessee River Valley.

The Overhill Cherokee lived in towns along the Little Tennessee and upper Tennessee Rivers; Chota was their main town. Women farmed the family land and children belonged to their mother's clan, and corn was honored in the Green Corn Ceremony.

The Chickasaw homeland included West Tennessee, northern Mississippi, and nearby lands. They were known as traders, women controlled most property, and in 1540 they met, and later nearly destroyed, de Soto's Spanish force.
Spanish explorers also met Shawnee people in the region; the Cherokee later pushed the Creek, Yuchi, and Shawnee out.

first_peoples.today_note: Tennessee has no federally recognized tribe today. The Cherokee were forced west on the Trail of Tears; their nations today are the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians, both based in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, and the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, whose land in North Carolina borders the Great Smoky Mountains. The Chickasaw Nation is headquartered in Ada, Oklahoma.
sites: Red Clay, Tennessee: the last Eastern capital of the Cherokee Nation, where the Trail of Tears began
Great Smoky Mountains National Park (the Cherokee called the range Shaconage, "place of blue smoke")
The Little Tennessee River, home of the Overhill Cherokee towns of Chota and Tanasi

history.event: Paleoindians are living in Tennessee by about 13,000 years ago, hunting Ice Age animals such as mastodons.
Mississippian chiefdoms build ceremonial structures across Tennessee.
Hernando de Soto's Spanish expedition meets the Chickasaw and other nations.
Spanish captain Juan Pardo records a village called "Tanasqui," the likely root of the name Tennessee.
Fort Loudoun is built in Cherokee country; it surrenders in 1760 after a siege.
Dragging Canoe's Chickamauga Cherokee, allied with the British, attack Fort Watauga, where settlers had moved onto Cherokee land. Nancy Ward's warnings save many settlers' lives.
Settlers build Fort Nashborough, which grows into Nashville.
North Carolina gives the land to the federal government and it becomes the Southwest Territory; 3,417 enslaved people already live there.
On June 1, Tennessee becomes the 16th state.
Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby get the Chickasaw to agree to sell their land between the Tennessee and Mississippi Rivers (the Jackson Purchase).

Removal: Chickasaw families gather at Memphis in 1837 to be moved west. In 1838-1839 U.S. troops force about 17,000 Cherokee from camps such as Fort Cass onto the Trail of Tears ("the Trail Where We Cried"); about 4,000 die.
Enslaved people make up about one in four Tennesseans.

Voters approve secession on June 8, 1861, making Tennessee the last state to join the Confederacy, but much of East Tennessee stays loyal to the Union and about 30,000 Tennessee men fight for the Union. About 2,900 battles and skirmishes take place in the state, including Shiloh (1862), Chattanooga (1863), and Franklin and Nashville (1864).
Tennessee ends slavery by changing its own state constitution (approved by voters in March) and ratifies the 13th Amendment on April 7.

Fisk University opens in Nashville to educate freed people, and the Ku Klux Klan is organized in Pulaski. From April 30 to May 1, white mobs in Memphis kill 46 Black men, women, and children and destroy all of the city's Black churches and schools (the Memphis Massacre); news of the violence built support for Radical Republicans in Congress, who pushed for stronger civil rights. On July 24 Tennessee becomes the first former Confederate state to have its members seated again in Congress.

trailblazers.name: Nancy Ward
trailblazers.text: Nancy Ward was an Overhill Cherokee woman and a cousin of the war leader Dragging Canoe. In 1776 she warned settlers that attacks were coming, which saved many lives.

trailblazers.name: Sequoyah
trailblazers.text: Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who spoke no English, began around 1809 to create a way to write the Cherokee language. His syllabary, introduced in 1821, spread so fast that by the 1820s more Cherokee could read and write than their white neighbors in Georgia. The Cherokee Phoenix newspaper later printed in it.

trailblazers.name: Andrew Jackson
trailblazers.text: Jackson became a hero after winning the Battle of New Orleans in 1815 and was president from 1829 to 1837. At his Nashville plantation, the Hermitage, he enslaved more than 150 people by the time he died. As president he signed the Indian Removal Act of 1830, which forced tens of thousands of Native people from their homelands and led to the Trail of Tears.

trailblazers.name: The Fisk Jubilee Singers
trailblazers.text: Fisk University was founded in Nashville in 1866 to educate formerly enslaved people. Its student choir, the Fisk Jubilee Singers, helped bring African American spirituals to wide audiences.

trailblazers.name: Ida B. Wells
trailblazers.group: Black American woman, journalist and civil rights leader
trailblazers.text: In 1883 Wells refused to give up her seat on a train, was forced off, and sued the railroad; she won $500, but the Tennessee Supreme Court overturned the ruling in 1885. She bought a one-third share of the Memphis Free Speech newspaper and, after three Black owners of the People's Grocery were lynched in 1892, wrote about the killings. A white mob destroyed the paper's office, and after threats she moved to Chicago and kept fighting lynching.

trailblazers.name: Anne Dallas Dudley
trailblazers.text: In 1911 Dudley helped found the Nashville Equal Suffrage League and became its president, and she led suffrage parades, often with her two young daughters. In 1915 she was elected president of the Tennessee Equal Suffrage Association. On August 18, 1920, Tennessee became the 36th and final state needed to ratify the 19th Amendment, giving women the right to vote.

trailblazers.name: Wilma Rudolph
trailblazers.text: Rudolph was born in Clarksville, the twentieth of twenty-two children. After polio, she wore leg braces from age six to ten. Coach Ed Temple of Tennessee A&I State College (now Tennessee State University) invited her to his track camp at age fourteen, and at the 1960 Rome Olympics she won three gold medals.

landforms: Great Smoky Mountains and Blue Ridge
Kuwohi (formerly Clingmans Dome), highest point at about 6,643 feet
Ridge and Valley (Great Valley, home of Knoxville and Chattanooga)
Gulf Coastal Plain and Mississippi Alluvial Plain
waters: Mississippi River (western border; lowest point at 178 feet)
Reelfoot Lake (formed by the 1811-1812 New Madrid earthquakes)
geography.regions: Three Grand Divisions: mountainous East Tennessee, the plateau and basin of Middle Tennessee, and the low plains of West Tennessee along the Mississippi River.

ecosystems.name: Great Smoky Mountains forest
ecosystems.about: Forest covers about 95 percent of the park, and its cove hardwood forests hold more than 130 kinds of trees. About 1,900 black bears live there.

ecosystems.name: Salamander streams
ecosystems.about: The Smokies are called the "Salamander Capital of the World," with up to 31 salamander species.

ecosystems.name: Reelfoot Lake wetlands
ecosystems.about: An earthquake-made lake in northwest Tennessee, known for its standing tree stumps and a lotus bed.

science.weather: Mostly humid subtropical with about 50 inches of rain and snow a year. About 15 tornadoes a year, mostly in West and Middle Tennessee, plus thunderstorms, ice storms, and mountain fog. The New Madrid earthquakes of 1811-1812 shook West Tennessee.
science.resources: Cattle, soybeans, poultry, corn, and cotton; zinc and marble; Tennessee Valley Authority dams and power plants; plus health care, music, the auto industry, and tourism.
science.highlight: Great Smoky Mountains National Park is the most biologically diverse national park in the country, with about 19,000 known species and maybe 80,000 to 100,000 more still unknown. Its synchronous fireflies (Photinus carolinus) flash together each late May to early June near Elkmont.
